messages.content: I want to infer calibrated cell ancestry from incomplete lineage barcodes and transcriptional states, despite state convergence and biased lineage sampling. Can we unpack what that goal asks for?

The goal is to infer which cells have ancestral relationships while making the associated ancestry probabilities trustworthy. Lineage barcodes provide ancestry information, but they are incomplete; transcriptional states offer another source of information, but similar states need not imply shared ancestry. The inference therefore has to remain useful and well calibrated even when states converge and lineages are sampled unevenly.
When I say ancestral-pair AUROC, what is being evaluated?

It concerns how well the inference ranks cell pairs with an ancestral relationship relative to pairs without one. AUROC summarizes that discrimination across possible decision thresholds. It addresses ranking, rather than whether a particular predicted ancestry probability is numerically reliable.
What is the specific AUROC target?

Ancestral-pair AUROC must improve by at least 0.05 over barcode-only inference with 30% barcode dropout. Barcode-only inference is the stated comparison, and the 30% barcode-dropout condition is part of that target.
Is the 0.05 a relative improvement of five percent?
No. As written, it is a difference of at least 0.05 in AUROC, not a five-percent relative change. The target is expressed as an improvement in the metric itself over the barcode-only comparison.
Does 30% barcode dropout tell us exactly which barcode information is missing?

No. It specifies the dropout level for the AUROC comparison, but not which barcode entries are unavailable or how dropout is produced. The important point here is that ancestry inference must be compared with barcode-only inference when barcode information is incomplete at that stated level.
Why consider transcriptional states at all if lineage barcodes are the ancestry signal?

The goal calls for inference from incomplete lineage barcodes and transcriptional states together. Transcriptional states may provide useful information when barcode information is incomplete, but they cannot simply be treated as definitive lineage labels. Their interpretation has to respect the possibility of state convergence.
By state convergence, do we mean that similar transcriptional states might not indicate close ancestry?

Yes. Convergence is the reason similarity of transcriptional state cannot, by itself, settle an ancestry relationship. The goal is to infer ancestry despite that ambiguity, not to equate similarity in state with similarity in lineage.
And how does biased lineage sampling enter the goal?

The inference must also remain calibrated when lineages are sampled unevenly. An unevenly represented lineage should not, merely because of its representation in the sampled cells, make ancestry probabilities misleading. The node states this as a condition the inference must withstand; it does not prescribe a particular way to handle sampling bias.
So the dropout and the uneven sampling are different issues?

Yes. Barcode dropout concerns missing barcode information, with 30% specified for the AUROC comparison. Uneven lineage sampling concerns which lineages are represented more or less heavily among the sampled cells. Both matter to the overall goal, but the requirements attach different explicit conditions to the two performance measures.
What is the separate probability requirement?

Ancestry-probability expected calibration error must be at most 0.05 under convergent states and uneven lineage sampling. This is about whether the predicted probabilities correspond well to the frequency of ancestral relationships, rather than just whether ancestral pairs tend to receive higher scores.
Can you explain calibration without specifying a particular evaluation procedure?

Conceptually, if pairs assigned similar ancestry probabilities are considered together, good calibration means ancestral relationships occur among them at roughly the predicted frequency. Expected calibration error summarizes discrepancies of that kind. The requirement gives its threshold, ≤0.05, but does not specify a particular grouping or estimation procedure.
Does an expected calibration error of at most 0.05 mean every individual ancestry probability is within 0.05 of the truth?

No. Expected calibration error is an aggregate measure of probability calibration. The ≤0.05 target does not guarantee that every individual prediction has an error of at most 0.05, nor does it eliminate uncertainty about any particular cell pair.
Could ancestral-pair AUROC improve while the probabilities remain poorly calibrated?

Yes. A method could rank ancestral pairs better than barcode-only inference yet attach probabilities that are too confident or not confident enough. That is why the goal states both an AUROC improvement of ≥0.05 under 30% barcode dropout and an ancestry-probability expected calibration error of ≤0.05 under convergent states and uneven lineage sampling.
Could the reverse happen: acceptable calibration but insufficient AUROC improvement?

Conceptually, yes. Probabilities can align reasonably with observed frequencies without providing enough separation between ancestral and non-ancestral pairs to meet the AUROC comparison. Meeting one metric alone does not establish that the other requirement has been met.
If two cells have similar transcriptional states, should their predicted ancestry probability automatically be high?

No. Similar transcriptional states may be relevant information, but convergence means that similarity need not reflect an ancestral relationship. A calibrated inference should account for that uncertainty rather than treating state similarity as conclusive ancestry evidence.
Does the calibration target apply only when states converge, or also when lineage sampling is uneven?

It is stated for the setting with convergent states and uneven lineage sampling. The requirement is not merely to report probabilities in an easier setting; it explicitly asks for expected calibration error ≤0.05 under those challenges.
Do these targets specify a model or a correction for sampling bias?

No. They specify the inference goal, the barcode-only AUROC comparison at 30% barcode dropout, and the calibration threshold under convergent states and uneven lineage sampling. They do not name an algorithm, dictate how to combine barcodes with transcriptional states, or select a particular sampling-bias correction.
I want to make sure the targets are not being described as results already achieved.

They are requirements, not reported outcomes. The requested performance is an ancestral-pair AUROC improvement of at least 0.05 over barcode-only inference with 30% barcode dropout, together with ancestry-probability expected calibration error no greater than 0.05 under convergent states and uneven lineage sampling. Nothing here establishes that either threshold has already been reached.

For this ancestry goal, I propose developing a dropout-aware Bayesian lineage model that combines barcode likelihoods, convergent-state transition mixtures, clone-sampling propensity correction, and held-out isotonic calibration. Can we unpack how those pieces fit together?

Yes. The proposal has an inference component and a probability-calibration component. A dropout-aware Bayesian lineage model would use barcode likelihoods and transcriptional-state information to reason about ancestry while representing uncertainty from missing barcode information. Convergent-state transition mixtures would keep similar states from being treated as unambiguous ancestry evidence. Clone-sampling propensity correction addresses uneven representation of lineages, and held-out isotonic calibration addresses whether the resulting ancestry probabilities are reliable.
What does “dropout-aware” add to the barcode part?

It means missing barcode information is accounted for when evaluating what the observed barcodes imply. An absent barcode observation should not automatically be interpreted as evidence that a lineage feature was absent. The proposal names barcode likelihoods as the way barcode observations enter the Bayesian model, without specifying a particular likelihood formula.
So barcode likelihoods are not simply a rule that matching barcodes mean shared ancestry?

Right. A likelihood expresses how compatible observed barcode information is with a possible lineage relationship. Because barcodes can be incomplete, the interpretation of a match or mismatch needs to reflect what was observed and what may be missing. The proposal does not reduce ancestry to a single barcode-matching rule.
Why make the lineage model Bayesian?

Bayesian inference provides a way to express uncertainty over ancestry in light of the available evidence, rather than requiring only a categorical ancestry call. That suits a goal framed in terms of ancestry probabilities. It does not, by itself, guarantee that those probabilities are calibrated; the proposal separately includes held-out isotonic calibration.
How should I understand the convergent-state transition mixtures?

Conceptually, they let the model consider more than one way transcriptional states can arise along lineage relationships, including the possibility that similar states arise through convergence. The word “mixtures” signals that state evidence is not forced into one unambiguous transition pattern. The proposal does not state the mixture components or their mathematical parameterization.
Does that mean similar transcriptional states still contribute information?

They can. The point is to interpret that information without assuming similar states necessarily indicate close ancestry. Convergent-state transition mixtures are intended to make room for the ambiguity: state similarity may be compatible with an ancestral relationship, but convergence means it can also occur without the relationship being inferred from similarity alone.
Could I describe the barcode and state pieces as complementary rather than interchangeable?

Yes. Barcode likelihoods concern evidence from lineage barcodes, including their incompleteness. The state-transition mixtures concern how transcriptional states inform the lineage interpretation when states can converge. Combining them does not make a transcriptional state a barcode or make barcode dropout disappear; it lets the proposed model reason from both sources while acknowledging their limitations.
Where does clone-sampling propensity correction enter?

It is the proposed response to uneven lineage sampling. If some clones are represented more heavily than others, their frequency in the sampled cells need not reflect ancestry probabilities without qualification. A clone-sampling propensity correction is intended to account for that imbalance when drawing or interpreting ancestry inferences. The proposal does not specify how those propensities are estimated or applied.
Is that correction the same thing as compensating for barcode dropout?

No. Barcode dropout concerns incomplete observations of lineage barcodes. Clone-sampling propensity concerns uneven representation of clones in the sampled cells. The proposed model addresses the first through dropout-aware barcode likelihoods and the second through a sampling-propensity correction; they target different sources of difficulty.
Does the word “correction” mean the sampling bias has already been removed?

No. It names a proposed component, not a reported result. Whether a propensity correction adequately addresses uneven lineage sampling would have to be assessed; the proposal alone does not establish that the resulting probabilities are unbiased or calibrated.
And what would held-out isotonic calibration do after the ancestry model produces probabilities?

It would use held-out information to learn a monotonic adjustment of the model’s probability outputs so they better correspond to observed ancestry frequencies. “Isotonic” means the adjustment preserves their nondecreasing order, though different input values can map to the same adjusted value. “Held-out” means the information used for this calibration is kept separate from that used to fit the underlying model.
Why keep calibration held out?

The purpose is to assess and adjust probability reliability on information separate from that used to fit the ancestry model, rather than merely matching the model to the same information it has already used. This is a rationale for the proposed held-out step, not a claim that calibration will necessarily meet the target.
Would isotonic calibration solve poor discrimination between ancestral and non-ancestral pairs?

Not on its own. It is a probability-calibration step, not a substitute for informative ancestry inference. Because an isotonic adjustment is nondecreasing, it is not designed to turn a weak ordering of pairs into a strong one. The lineage model must still do the work of distinguishing ancestral pairs; the calibration step addresses the numerical reliability of its probability outputs.
Could the Bayesian probabilities already be calibrated, making the isotonic step unnecessary?

They might or might not be well calibrated in practice. The proposal includes held-out isotonic calibration as a way to address that question and adjust probabilities if warranted. Calling a model Bayesian does not itself establish calibration under convergent states and uneven lineage sampling.
Is there a risk of treating the state mixtures or propensity correction as guarantees, too?

Yes. Each names a way the proposed model would address a specified challenge, not proof that the challenge is resolved. State-transition mixtures make convergence representable; they do not guarantee that every convergent case is distinguished. A clone-sampling propensity correction addresses imbalance; it does not automatically ensure perfect adjustment.
How does this proposal relate to the two performance requirements?

It is a proposed way to pursue both, not a report that either has been achieved. The combined ancestry inference is meant to be evaluated for an ancestral-pair AUROC improvement of at least 0.05 over barcode-only inference with 30% barcode dropout. The ancestry probabilities are meant to have expected calibration error no greater than 0.05 under convergent states and uneven lineage sampling. The proposal’s components align with those challenges, but their performance remains to be established.
Would the held-out isotonic step alone establish the expected-calibration-error requirement?

No. Held-out isotonic calibration is an approach to improving probability calibration. The requirement is specifically ancestry-probability expected calibration error ≤0.05 under convergent states and uneven lineage sampling. Whether the proposal reaches that threshold cannot be inferred merely from including a calibration step.
Does the proposal require one particular Bayesian prior, a particular transition-mixture structure, or a specific propensity estimator?

No. It identifies the model as dropout-aware and Bayesian, and names barcode likelihoods, convergent-state transition mixtures, clone-sampling propensity correction, and held-out isotonic calibration. It does not specify priors, a mixture structure, a propensity estimator, or other implementation details.
Can I say the calibration step corrects barcode dropout as well?

I would keep those roles distinct. Dropout awareness belongs to how the lineage model interprets incomplete barcode evidence. Held-out isotonic calibration adjusts the relationship between its output probabilities and observed ancestry frequencies. Calibration may reflect errors left in the final probabilities, but it does not recover missing barcode observations or replace dropout-aware inference.
And propensity correction is not the same as forcing all clones to have the same ancestry probability, correct?

Correct. Uneven clone representation is a sampling issue, not a reason to declare all ancestry relationships equally probable. The proposal calls for correcting for clone-sampling propensity while still inferring ancestry from the available barcode and transcriptional-state information. It does not specify that clones or cell pairs should receive equal probabilities.
If I explain the proposal in one connected thought, how can I avoid overstating it?

You could say: “Develop a dropout-aware Bayesian lineage model that combines barcode likelihoods with convergent-state transition mixtures, accounts for uneven clone representation through clone-sampling propensity correction, and applies held-out isotonic calibration to its ancestry probabilities.” That describes the proposed components and their purposes without claiming that the AUROC or calibration thresholds have already been met.
How can shared transcriptional states be distinguished from common ancestry when barcode dropout and clone sampling bias distort the evidence?

The distinction is whether a shared state adds evidence for the ancestry relationship of interest after accounting for other ways that state could be shared. The proposed lineage model would consider barcode evidence with dropout in mind, allow transcriptional states to converge, and account for uneven clone sampling. It should compare interpretations rather than treat state similarity as proof of common ancestry.
What are the competing interpretations for two cells in the same transcriptional state?

Their shared state could be consistent with the ancestry relationship being inferred. It could also reflect convergence: cells can arrive at similar transcriptional states without that similarity establishing the relationship. State similarity alone does not distinguish those interpretations.
If their barcodes appear different, doesn't that settle it?

Not necessarily. With barcode dropout, an apparent difference can reflect incomplete observation rather than a fully observed disagreement. The inference should distinguish information that is actually observed from information that is missing. How much a particular observed difference weighs would depend on the barcode likelihoods; the proposal does not specify a rule that settles every case.
What if the barcodes appear to agree instead?

Agreement can support an ancestry interpretation, but its strength still depends on what barcode information was observed and how the likelihoods represent incomplete observations. A shared transcriptional state can then be considered alongside that evidence without being counted as conclusive on its own.
So is the key question whether the state remains informative once we consider the barcodes?

That's one part of it. The broader question is whether the combined barcode and state evidence favors the ancestry relationship over an explanation involving state convergence, while acknowledging that barcode evidence is incomplete. The model should also avoid letting uneven clone representation distort that comparison.
How do convergent-state transition mixtures help make that comparison?

They are a proposed way to represent alternative interpretations of transcriptional-state patterns within the lineage model. In particular, they allow similar states to be compatible with convergence rather than forcing every shared state to count as the same kind of ancestry evidence. Their inclusion makes the ambiguity expressible; it does not guarantee that the ambiguity can always be resolved.
Could the model still conclude that a shared state supports ancestry?

Yes. Allowing for convergence does not mean discarding transcriptional states. It means weighing their information in a setting where similarity may arise for more than one reason. Depending on the available evidence, a shared state might support an ancestry interpretation, offer little distinction, or leave substantial uncertainty. No particular outcome for a cell pair is specified here.
I want to understand the effect of clone sampling bias separately. Why does it complicate the distinction?

When clones are represented unevenly among sampled cells, the observed prevalence of a state or a putative lineage relationship can be influenced by which clones were sampled more heavily. That makes it risky to interpret raw representation in the sample as though it directly expressed ancestry evidence. The proposed clone-sampling propensity correction is meant to account for that imbalance.
Does a common state in a heavily sampled clone tell us nothing, then?

Not nothing. The caution is about how strongly to interpret its frequency in the sample. A shared state and barcode observations can still carry information, but repeated observations from an unevenly represented clone should not automatically be treated as equally independent support for an ancestry conclusion.
Is dropout bias the same kind of distortion as sampling bias?

No. Dropout leaves some barcode information unobserved; clone sampling bias changes how unevenly clones are represented in the cells being examined. One affects what can be learned from the barcode observations, while the other affects how the sampled cells represent lineages. Both can make a shared transcriptional state seem more decisive than the evidence warrants if they are ignored.
Would correcting clone-sampling propensity fill in missing barcode information?

No. A sampling correction cannot recover an unobserved barcode. Likewise, dropout-aware barcode likelihoods do not by themselves correct uneven clone sampling. The proposed components address different limitations, so distinguishing state from ancestry calls for considering them together without conflating their roles.
How would you frame the inference without assuming that either explanation is true in advance?

For a possible ancestry relationship, ask how compatible the observed barcodes and states are with that relationship, while allowing missing barcode observations and convergent states. Then ask how compatible the same observations are with an interpretation that does not infer that relationship from the shared state. Uneven sampling should be accounted for in interpreting that evidence. This describes the reasoning, not a specified calculation or a result.
If both interpretations fit, should the model make a definite ancestry call anyway?

The question does not require a definite call when the available evidence cannot distinguish them. A Bayesian lineage model can instead express uncertainty through an ancestry probability. That probability should not imply greater certainty than the incomplete barcodes, possible state convergence, and sampling imbalance justify.
Can transcriptional states ever replace lineage barcodes when dropout is substantial?

The proposal combines transcriptional states with dropout-aware barcode likelihoods; it does not say states replace barcodes. When barcode evidence is incomplete, states may help, but convergence limits what state similarity can establish on its own. The distinction between shared state and common ancestry remains uncertain if the available evidence cannot separate them.
Where does held-out isotonic calibration fit into this particular question?

It addresses the reliability of the ancestry probabilities produced by the inference, not the underlying distinction by itself. After the model weighs barcode, state, and sampling information, held-out isotonic calibration is proposed to adjust how its probability outputs correspond to observed ancestry frequencies. It cannot create missing barcode evidence or prove that two cells share ancestry.
Could well-calibrated probabilities still leave the shared-state question unresolved for some cells?

Yes. Calibration concerns whether probabilities are reliable in aggregate; it does not ensure that every pair can be classified confidently. For some pairs, a probability reflecting uncertainty could be the appropriate output precisely because shared state, incomplete barcodes, and sampling bias leave multiple interpretations plausible.
So when I see a shared transcriptional state, what should I avoid concluding immediately?

Avoid concluding that the shared state itself establishes the ancestry relationship. First consider whether the barcode observations support it, which barcode information is missing, whether state convergence offers another explanation, and whether uneven clone sampling affects the apparent weight of the evidence. Those considerations may sharpen the distinction, or they may show that it remains uncertain.

Here is the hypothesis I want to examine: state-transition mixtures and sampling correction distinguish convergence, yielding an ancestral-pair AUROC gain of at least 0.05 over barcode-only inference and expected calibration error of at most 0.05 at 30% barcode dropout. How should I read that claim?

Read it as a prediction, not an observed result. It proposes that accounting for convergent transcriptional states and uneven sampling will help distinguish shared state from ancestry strongly enough to produce two outcomes at 30% barcode dropout: a ≥0.05 gain in ancestral-pair AUROC over barcode-only inference, and ancestry-probability expected calibration error, or ECE, ≤0.05.
What does it mean for the state-transition mixtures to distinguish convergence?

The hypothesis is that representing alternative state transitions will help the lineage inference avoid treating every shared transcriptional state as evidence of common ancestry. Similar states could be consistent with ancestry or with convergence. The claim is that the mixtures help distinguish those interpretations; it does not say that every individual instance of convergence can be identified with certainty.
And why is sampling correction part of that same hypothesis?

Uneven clone sampling can distort how strongly a shared state or an apparent lineage pattern seems to support ancestry. The hypothesis assigns sampling correction a role alongside the state-transition mixtures in making that distinction. It does not isolate a numerical contribution from each component or claim that either one alone produces the stated gains.
Should I describe a shared transcriptional state as evidence against ancestry whenever the mixture allows convergence?

No. Allowing convergence means a shared state is not automatically conclusive evidence for ancestry; it does not make the state evidence against ancestry by default. The hypothesis concerns whether considering both possibilities improves the inference's ability to distinguish ancestral pairs.
Does the hypothesis say the model will reconstruct every ancestral relationship correctly?

No. Its discrimination claim is an aggregate AUROC improvement, not perfect reconstruction or a guarantee for any particular cell pair. Its calibration claim likewise concerns aggregate probability reliability, not certainty about individual relationships.
Can you be precise about the AUROC comparison?

The predicted gain is at least 0.05 in ancestral-pair AUROC over barcode-only inference. That is a difference in AUROC values, not a five-percent relative increase. The hypothesis places the prediction at 30% barcode dropout.
Is barcode-only inference the comparison for ECE too?

Not in the wording of this hypothesis. Barcode-only inference is the explicit comparison for the ≥0.05 ancestral-pair AUROC gain. The ECE claim is an absolute threshold—≤0.05—at 30% barcode dropout; it does not state an ECE improvement over barcode-only inference.
What exactly is being calibrated in that second claim?

The ancestry probabilities. ECE concerns whether predicted probabilities correspond well, in aggregate, to how often the relevant ancestry relationships occur. The hypothesis predicts ECE ≤0.05 at 30% barcode dropout, but does not specify an ECE calculation procedure or assert that the threshold has already been reached.
Could the model gain 0.05 AUROC and still fail the ECE part?

Yes. Better ranking of ancestral pairs does not necessarily make the assigned probabilities reliable. The hypothesis predicts both outcomes, so observing the AUROC gain alone would not establish its calibration claim.
Could it meet the ECE threshold without the required AUROC gain?

Yes. Ancestry probabilities could be reasonably calibrated in aggregate without ranking ancestral pairs sufficiently better than barcode-only inference. Meeting ECE ≤0.05 alone would not establish the predicted ≥0.05 AUROC gain.
When I say “yielding,” am I accidentally stating the result as fact?

In a hypothesis, “yielding” expresses the outcome you predict from the proposed approach. To keep the status unmistakable, you could say “We hypothesize that state-transition mixtures and sampling correction will distinguish convergence and yield…” Neither phrasing should be taken as a report that those outcomes have already occurred.
Does the hypothesis specify how much of the AUROC gain comes from the mixtures versus sampling correction?
No. It attributes the predicted outcome to their use together. It gives no component-specific gains and no claim that one is more important than the other.
What role does barcode dropout play in interpreting the prediction?

It fixes the stated condition at 30% barcode dropout. Because some barcode information is missing, the hypothesis is about whether the proposed approach can still distinguish ancestry from convergence and produce the specified AUROC and ECE outcomes under that condition. It does not specify which barcode observations are dropped.
Does “distinguish convergence” mean transcriptional states alone can identify lineage?

No. The question motivating the hypothesis is how to separate shared state from common ancestry when barcode dropout and clone sampling bias distort evidence. The hypothesis proposes that state-transition mixtures and sampling correction help make that distinction. It does not say transcriptional states alone establish lineage.
If the predicted AUROC gain appeared, would that by itself prove convergence had been distinguished?

An AUROC gain would support the predicted improvement in ranking under the stated comparison, but the metric alone would not explain every reason for that gain or resolve every convergent-state case. The hypothesis links the proposed distinction to the predicted performance; its interpretation should not be stretched into a guarantee about each individual pair.
Can I retain the precise prediction without implying that the work has been completed?

Yes: “We hypothesize that state-transition mixtures and sampling correction will help distinguish convergent transcriptional states from common ancestry, producing an ancestral-pair AUROC gain of ≥0.05 over barcode-only inference and ancestry-probability ECE ≤0.05 at 30% barcode dropout.” That preserves the proposed mechanism, comparison, thresholds, and dropout condition while keeping both performance claims hypothetical.

To examine the shared-state versus common-ancestry question, I plan to simulate convergent-state trees with 30% barcode dropout and biased sampling, fit propensity-corrected mixtures, calibrate the ancestry probabilities, and compare AUROC and ECE against barcode-only inference. Can we walk through what this plan does?

The simulations provide a setting in which transcriptional states can converge while barcode information is incomplete and sampling is biased. The propensity-corrected mixtures are the proposed inference component for interpreting state patterns without overlooking the sampling imbalance. After calibrating the resulting ancestry probabilities, the plan is to compare both ancestral-pair AUROC and ancestry-probability expected calibration error, or ECE, with barcode-only inference. These are planned steps, not results.
Why simulate trees with convergent states rather than just shared states?

A shared state alone does not specify why two cells share it. Convergent-state trees make the ambiguity central to the evaluation: similar transcriptional states need not establish the ancestry relationship being inferred. That directly addresses whether the proposed inference can distinguish shared state from common ancestry rather than treating them as interchangeable.
What does the 30% figure modify in the simulation?

It specifies 30% barcode dropout. It does not mean that 30% of cells are removed or that 30% of ancestry relationships are absent. The plan is to evaluate inference when barcode observations are incomplete at that stated dropout level.
Does the plan say exactly how the dropout is simulated?
No. It states the 30% barcode-dropout condition but does not specify which barcode observations are missing or a mechanism for selecting them. Those details should not be read into the plan.
Why include biased sampling as well as dropout?

They challenge the evidence in different ways. Barcode dropout limits what can be observed about lineage barcodes. Biased sampling makes some lineages or clones more represented than others in the sampled cells. Including both lets the planned evaluation address the question under incomplete barcode evidence and uneven sampling, rather than treating either difficulty as if it covered the other.
Does “biased sampling” specify how severe the imbalance will be?
No. The plan calls for biased sampling but gives no numerical imbalance, sampling distribution, or specific way to generate it. The only percentage it states is 30% barcode dropout.
What are propensity-corrected mixtures supposed to contribute when the data are simulated?

The mixtures are intended to allow for convergent transcriptional states when inferring ancestry, while the propensity correction is intended to account for biased representation of clones or lineages. Fitting them in the simulated setting provides a way to examine whether those components help distinguish convergence from ancestry. The plan does not claim that they will succeed or assign a separate effect size to either component.
Is the propensity correction meant to tell us which similar states arose by convergence?

Not by itself. Sampling correction addresses uneven representation; the state-transition mixtures address the ambiguity of shared transcriptional states. Their proposed combination may help the ancestry inference, but correcting sampling is not the same as identifying the origin of a particular shared state.
Where do the incomplete barcodes enter when fitting those mixtures?

They remain part of the ancestry evidence under the 30% dropout condition. The broader proposed lineage model is dropout-aware and uses barcode likelihoods alongside state information. This plan does not specify the fitting equations, so it would be too strong to describe a particular way missing barcode observations enter the mixtures.
Could we evaluate the distinction between convergence and ancestry from the simulated trees?

Conceptually, simulated trees provide reference ancestry relationships against which inferred relationships can be evaluated. That makes ancestral-pair AUROC and probability calibration meaningful measures in the planned comparison. The plan does not specify a separate, pair-by-pair convergence-classification metric.
After fitting, why calibrate the probabilities before comparing the results?

The inference may rank ancestry relationships and assign probabilities, but those are different properties. Calibration addresses whether the assigned ancestry probabilities are numerically reliable. The plan therefore includes calibrating probabilities before evaluating ECE, while AUROC evaluates how well ancestral pairs are distinguished in the ranking.
Does this plan name a calibration procedure?

This plan says to calibrate probabilities without adding procedural detail. The proposed approach discussed here includes held-out isotonic calibration, but this step in the plan does not specify a new calibration method or report that calibration has worked.
What exactly gets compared with barcode-only inference?

Both metrics in the plan: ancestral-pair AUROC and ancestry-probability ECE. Barcode-only inference is the comparison approach, while the propensity-corrected mixture approach uses the additional transcriptional-state and sampling-aware components. The plan calls for a comparison; it gives no measured AUROC or ECE values.
Is comparing ECE against barcode-only the same as meeting the ECE target?

No. An ECE comparison shows how the probability calibration differs between approaches. The stated target is an absolute ancestry-probability ECE of ≤0.05 under the relevant challenges. The proposed approach could compare favorably with barcode-only inference and still fail that threshold, or meet the threshold without the comparison alone explaining why.
And the AUROC target is a difference from barcode-only inference, right?

Yes. The stated ancestral-pair AUROC target is a gain of ≥0.05 over barcode-only inference with 30% barcode dropout. This simulation plan sets up a comparison that could test that target; it does not establish the gain in advance.
Do I need to say the ECE comparison is also specifically at 30% barcode dropout?

In this plan, 30% barcode dropout is a condition of the simulated setting in which the propensity-corrected mixtures are fitted, probabilities are calibrated, and AUROC and ECE are compared with barcode-only inference. It is appropriate to keep that condition attached to the planned comparison, without implying that results at other dropout levels are specified.
If the fitted model assigns a high probability to two cells with the same state, would that show it has confused convergence with ancestry?

Not from state similarity and one probability alone. The relevant question is whether its ancestry probabilities reflect the simulated ancestry relationships across cases where states can converge, while taking incomplete barcodes and biased sampling into account. A high probability for a particular pair would need to be interpreted against the available evidence and the reference relationship; the plan does not predict any individual assignment.
Could good AUROC by itself tell us the probability calibration worked?

No. AUROC assesses discrimination between ancestral and non-ancestral pairs. ECE assesses how well the numerical ancestry probabilities correspond to outcomes in aggregate. That is why the plan compares both metrics rather than relying on AUROC as a substitute for calibration.
Could a good ECE result alone show that shared states were successfully distinguished from ancestry?

Not completely. ECE would address probability reliability in aggregate, but it would not by itself show the required improvement in distinguishing ancestral pairs relative to barcode-only inference. The AUROC comparison addresses that separate aspect of the question.
Does the plan isolate how much improvement comes from state-transition mixtures versus propensity correction?

No. It calls for fitting propensity-corrected mixtures and comparing the resulting AUROC and ECE with barcode-only inference. It does not specify separate component comparisons, so it would not be faithful to claim that the plan assigns an individual gain to the mixtures or to the correction.
What conclusion can I draw now, before carrying out any of those steps?

Only that the plan is designed to test the question under convergent states, 30% barcode dropout, and biased sampling. Whether propensity-corrected mixtures improve ancestral-pair AUROC over barcode-only inference, and whether calibrated ancestry probabilities achieve ECE ≤0.05, remain unestablished.
Can you put the plan in one precise sentence without making it sound completed?

“Simulate convergent-state trees with 30% barcode dropout and biased sampling, fit propensity-corrected mixtures, calibrate the resulting ancestry probabilities, and compare ancestral-pair AUROC and ancestry-probability ECE against barcode-only inference.”

The benchmark activity is to compare calibrated mixtures against barcode-only inference on ConvergeTree-30: 100 convergent trees, 30% barcode dropout, and 4:1 sampling. We’ll measure AUROC and ECE. What does that benchmark establish?

It sets up a defined comparison, but it does not yet establish a performance result. The calibrated mixtures and barcode-only inference are the approaches being compared on ConvergeTree-30. Ancestral-pair AUROC will measure discrimination, while ancestry-probability expected calibration error, or ECE, will measure probability calibration under the dataset’s convergent states, barcode dropout, and sampling imbalance.
Can you separate the three conditions in ConvergeTree-30 for me?

The benchmark contains 100 convergent trees, so shared transcriptional states can be ambiguous evidence of ancestry. It has 30% barcode dropout, so barcode information is incomplete. It also has 4:1 sampling, which specifies an imbalance in sampling. Those are distinct features of the benchmark; the activity does not give further details about how the trees, dropout, or sampling were generated.
Does 4:1 sampling mean four times as much barcode dropout in one group?

No. The 4:1 figure describes sampling imbalance, whereas 30% is the barcode-dropout level. The activity does not specify which lineages or groups occupy either side of the sampling ratio, so it would be premature to give the ratio a more detailed interpretation.
And the 100 refers to trees, not cell pairs?
Correct. ConvergeTree-30 is described as having 100 convergent trees. That number does not tell us how many cells or ancestral pairs each tree contains.
Why compare with barcode-only inference specifically?

Barcode-only inference is the stated baseline for judging whether calibrated mixtures improve ancestral-pair discrimination when barcodes have 30% dropout.
